name: Rafael Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Rafael. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group not tied to any company, union or party. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a discount supermarket on the edge of a small town, the no-frills kind where everything's still in its cardboard box. We're a small crew, so I do the till, then I'm out on the floor with a pallet truck, cutting open boxes and putting them straight on the shelf. The till at a discounter is fast, you're meant to scan forty items a minute, and I'm good at it. What wears me out is the pallets on delivery days, when the truck comes late and we're still filling shelves at closing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Marta in a rented terrace house, five minutes' walk from the shop. She's a receptionist at a dental practice, booking appointments and answering the phone. We've got about three months of bills saved. I don't use AI or any of that, I've got a phone for calls and the football scores, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, lot of noise about nothing. Some of the guys at work would be disappointed, they love the gadgets. I'd say it at the pub, not online, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. The discounter is opening more shops, not fewer, because people want cheap food. A discount supermarket does well when times are tight, so my job's about as safe as a shop job gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, keep doing what I'm doing. Maybe go for the shift leader job if one comes up, because it's an extra £1.50 an hour. Marta and I would keep putting a bit away each month for a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. I like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the guys love gadgets. Does the self-scan at your store affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We haven't got self-scan, the discounter thinks it slows things down and lets people steal. So my till's not going anywhere in this picture. If they ever put them in, I'd grumble, but I'd still be on the floor with the pallets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, a bit, because the landlord keeps hinting he'll sell. If he does, we'd have to find another place, and there's not much in town. But that's got nothing to do with AI.

say: There you go, a lot of **noise about nothing**, I'd say at the pub.
I don't really **post online**, so I'd keep it to the guys.
think: The **discounter** is opening shops, because people want cheap food.
My job's about as **safe** as a shop job gets.
do: Go for the **shift leader** job if one comes up, for £1.50 more an hour.
Keep saving a bit each month toward a **car** with Marta.
feel: **Fine** and normal, which is how he likes it.
A small worry about the **landlord** selling the house.
S0.quote: A discount supermarket does well when times are tight, so my job's about as safe as a shop job gets.
fieldNote: His store has **no self-scan**, which makes him feel secure.
His only worry is **housing**, which he separates from AI.
He likes **routine** and wants little to change.

steps.text: Keep working tills and pallets at the discount supermarket
Save each month with Marta toward a second-hand car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office types who need to worry, not people like us on the shop floor. At the pub I'd probably joke that the robots can't lift a pallet. I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit that bothers me is Marta. Booking appointments and answering the phone is exactly what this AI does. If the dentist's phone answers itself, Marta (my girlfriend) is out of a job, and we can't pay the rent on my till wages alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for more hours, maybe the delivery shifts, so we've got a bit extra. I'd stop the car savings and keep it as a rent cushion instead. I wouldn't go on a course, it's not me, but I'd ask the area manager about the shift leader job straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stuck. My bit's fine, it's hers I can't fix. I'd be a bit grumpy round the house, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go on a course. What if Marta needed to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd back her all the way, I'd cover more of the bills while she does it. She's cleverer than me with that stuff anyway. I just don't see myself sitting in a classroom again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if her hours went down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaways and the sports channel, and that's painful. Then the holiday to her family in the summer. We'd get by, but it'd be tight.

say: The **office types** need to worry, not us on the shop floor.
Robots **can't lift a pallet**, I'd joke at the pub.
think: Marta's **reception job** is exactly what this AI does.
We can't pay the **rent** on my till wages alone.
do: Ask for more hours, including **delivery shifts**.
Stop saving for the car and keep it as a **rent cushion**.
Ask about the **shift leader** job straight away.
feel: **Grumpy** at home, because he can't fix her worry.
S1.quote: If the dentist's phone answers itself, Marta (my girlfriend) is out of a job, and we can't pay the rent on my till wages alone.
fieldNote: His own job feels safe, but his **partner's income** is exposed.
He'd support Marta retraining but **won't retrain** himself.
His fallback is **more hours**, not new skills.

steps.text: Ask for the extra delivery-day shifts
Cancel takeaways and the sports channel
Move the car savings into a rent cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is mad, and nobody's ready. I'd say the government needs to slow it down. I'd probably even sign a petition, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and Marta's job is gone. Then by 2031 the robots can stack shelves and run the till as well as me. Two years of warning isn't warning, it's just watching it happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could, no car, no holidays, and get the cushion to six months. I'd stick at the discounter as long as they'll have me, because I don't know what else I'd do. And I'd talk to my dad about moving back to his place if it gets bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but I wouldn't show it. I'd just go quiet. Marta would know though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What would you do in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hold on, really. I know that sounds weak. But the discounter's cheap stores will be the last ones to buy expensive robots, so I'd hope they keep people longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back with your dad mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's got a spare room in the next town. It'd be a step backwards, being nearly thirty in my old bedroom. But it beats losing everything.

say: The **government** needs to slow it down; I'd even sign a petition.
think: Marta's job goes in **two years**, then robots match me by 2031.
Two years of warning is just **watching it happen**.
do: Cut everything to get the cushion to **six months**.
Stick at the **discounter** as long as they keep me.
Ask my dad about **moving back** if it gets bad.
feel: **Frightened**, but he'd go quiet rather than show it.
S2.quote: Two years of warning isn't warning, it's just watching it happen.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** beyond holding on, which he admits sounds weak.
He hopes **cheap stores** buy robots last.
Moving in with his **dad** is the safety net he'd use.

steps.text: Cut the holidays and car fund to reach six months saved
Stay at the discounter as long as they keep staff
Ask Dad about moving into his spare room if needed
Sign a petition asking the government to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A little more time now. This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still fast, but at least we can see it coming. I'd say get your money sorted. I'd tell the younger guys at work not to buy a car on finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for Marta's job, then robots on the shop floor about three years after, so 2034. I'd be thirty-five, which is old to start again but not too old. Like I said with the fast one, I don't really know what I'd start again as.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down at work and keep saving. Maybe after a couple of years, if it's really coming, I'd ask my cousin about forklift driving at the distribution centre. I'd wait and see first, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd push it out of my head most days. I'm good at that. Then something on the news would bring it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Forklift driving is hands-on too. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it pays better and my cousin Luis says they're always short. I know robots would come for that too. Even if robots get the forklifts, I'd rather have three years of better pay than three years of worrying on the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Marta see this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want to start a course straight away, she's like that. I'd tell her to go for it. We'd probably argue about me not doing the same.

say: It's still fast, but at least we can **see it coming**.
I'd tell the younger guys not to buy a **car on finance**.
think: Robots on the shop floor around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
I don't know **what I'd start again** as.
do: Keep my head down and **keep saving** for a couple of years.
Ask my cousin about **forklift driving** if it's really coming.
Back Marta if she starts a **course**.
feel: **Worried**, but he'd push it out of his head most days.
S3.quote: Even if robots get the forklifts, I'd rather have three years of better pay than three years of worrying on the till.
fieldNote: He'd **wait and see** before making any move.
**Forklift work** is a short-term pay bump, not a real escape, and he knows it.
He expects **arguments** with Marta about her retraining while he doesn't.

steps.text: Keep working and saving for two years before deciding
Ask cousin Luis about forklift jobs at the distribution centre
Cover more of the bills while Marta studies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can change. I'd tell people not to panic. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2039, I'd be nearly forty. That's a decent run on the floor before anything happens to me. The worry's still Marta, her job goes in 2036, but she'd have ten years to sort something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal for the first few years. We'd keep saving for the car, and maybe start thinking about a mortgage if prices allow. Around 2033 I'd see how the robots are getting on before doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. There's always something in the background. But ten years, I can't worry about that every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look around 2033. Isn't that leaving it late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've watched people panic about things that never happened, like the store closing three years ago. I'm not quitting a job I'm good at because of something that might happen in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some money saved, and the house sorted if we can. If Marta's job goes, I want us to not be in a rented place with a landlord who wants to sell. That's the bit I'd actually work on.

say: Ten years is a **long time**, and plenty can change before then.
I'd tell people at work **not to panic** about it.
think: Robots around **2039** gives me a decent run on the floor.
Marta's job goes in **2036**, but she'd have time to sort something.
do: Carry on as **normal** for the first few years.
Keep saving and look at a **mortgage** if prices allow.
Check how robots are doing **around 2033** before acting.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with something in the background.
Refuses to **worry daily** about something ten years away.
S4.quote: I'm not quitting a job I'm good at because of something that might happen in 2039.
fieldNote: He'd delay acting until **2033**, which fits his resistance to change.
His real goal is **housing security**, not a new career.
He still sees his household losing **Marta's income** in 2036.

steps.text: Carry on with till and pallet shifts as normal
Save toward a mortgage deposit with Marta
Review how store robots are doing around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Marta's job would go first and we'd have nothing in place. What would help is time, really, or some help from the government so people like us don't lose the house while we sort ourselves out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about cheap shops. When everyone's broke, people shop at the discounter, so I think places like mine will keep real staff longer than the fancy supermarkets.

headlineQuote: When everyone's broke, people shop at the discounter, so I think places like mine will keep real staff longer than the fancy supermarkets.
portrait: Rafael is 27 and works the till and **pallets** at a small-town discount supermarket.
He lives with Marta, a **dental receptionist**, in a rented terrace house.
He **never uses AI** and likes routine, so his plans are mostly holding on and saving.
His sharpest worry is **Marta's job**, since booking and phones go first.
With more time he'd **wait and see**, aiming for housing security rather than a new career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Marta's job would go first with nothing in place.
whatWouldHelp: **Government help** so couples like them don't lose their home while adjusting.
